title: IHG Hotels & Resorts Set to Debut First Kimpton Property in Indonesia
dek: Ubud is set to welcome a new chapter in luxury lifestyle hospitality with the arrival of Kimpton Suntaya Bali Ubud.
paras: Ubud is set to welcome a new chapter in luxury lifestyle hospitality with the arrival of Kimpton Suntaya Bali Ubud, marking IHG Hotels & Resorts’ first Kimpton property in Indonesia. Set along Jalan Bisma, the 101-key hotel is designed to capture the creative spirit and cultural rhythm of its surroundings.

Its name, Suntaya, reflects the balance at the heart of the concept, inspired by Sanskrit roots associated with stillness and vitality. Designed by Denton Corker Marshall with interiors by Threaded Creatives, the hotel follows Ubud’s natural contours, drawing inspiration from Balinese ceremonial processions and their sense of movement and community. Natural timber, locally sourced stone, handmade tiles, handcrafted details and curated Balinese art create a cohesive design rooted in the island’s craft and creative culture.

Kimpton Suntaya Bali Ubud will feature five dining destinations, two led by Michelin-starred Chef Hirofumi Imamura, including Imamura Ubud, an intimate omakase restaurant, and Shaku by Imamura, offering a refined take on Japanese izakaya dining. Wellness also takes centre stage, with a two-storey fitness studio named The Movement Lab, recovery facilities and contrast-therapy experiences, complemented by Sakshi, the resort’s spa offering Balinese-inspired treatments.

Guests can expect Kimpton signatures including the complimentary “Forgot It, We’ve Got It!” programme, inspiring conversation with other guests and the hotel’s management through Kimpton Morning Kickstart, and the convivial Kimpton Social.

Led by General Manager Austin Jones, who has contributed to nearly a dozen Kimpton properties, Kimpton Suntaya Bali Ubud is poised to become a new gathering place where travellers and locals can experience Ubud through a distinctly contemporary lens.

title: Savour Bold Indian Flavours at the Beachfront Tandoori Bar & Grill
dek: Indian cuisine takes a relaxed beachfront turn at Tandoori Bar & Grill, the newest dining destination at Karma Kandara.
paras: Indian cuisine takes a relaxed beachfront turn at Tandoori Bar & Grill, the newest dining destination at Karma Kandara. Designed as an all-day venue, the restaurant shifts effortlessly from casual afternoon bites to a more leisurely evening centred around the tandoor.

From 11am to 5pm, the menu at Tandoori Bar & Grill focuses on Indian street-food favourites, with Pav Bhaji, Vada Pav, Paneer Chilli and Chicken Tikka Kathi Rolls offering flavour-packed options for a relaxed daytime meal. As the sun begins to set, the kitchen moves into dinner service, with clay ovens taking centre stage alongside tandoor-grilled specialties, curries and generous sharing plates.

Highlights include Mushroom Tikka, Lamb Seekh Kebab and Chicken Tikka Kandhari, served with a mild pomegranate-yoghurt sauce. The menu also caters to plant-based diners with dishes such as smoky Baingan Bharta and classic Palak Paneer, while meat lovers can turn to Butter Chicken or the slow-cooked Laal Maas mutton curry. Biryani, freshly baked breads, rice, raita, salads and traditional desserts complement the offering.

At the helm is Chef Jeevraj Singh, whose culinary story began in his grandmother’s kitchen in Rajasthan before taking him through royal palaces and international kitchens, including Karma properties across India and Germany. His cooking remains grounded in the traditions of his homeland while reflecting the places he has travelled.
Access to the private members’ club area requires complimentary Karma Club Guest Membership registration via the Karma Subito App, which also includes dining, beverage and spa benefits.
For more information or reservations, please contact +62 361 848 2200 or follow @tandoori.bar.and.grill for updates.

title: Catch & Grill the Ocean's Bounty at Sofitel Bali Nusa Dua Beach Resort
dek: Sofitel Bali Nusa Dua Beach Resort invites guests to experience Bali’s coastal bounty in a more immersive way with Catch & Grill.
paras: Sofitel Bali Nusa Dua Beach Resort invites guests to experience Bali’s coastal bounty in a more immersive way with Catch & Grill. This new ocean-to-table dining experience pairs a traditional fishing excursion with a freshly prepared beachfront feast.

The Catch & Grill experience begins at sunrise with a private fishing trip aboard a local boat, departing at 7am. As guests venture out onto the waters, they can enjoy a leisurely morning casting lines while taking in the tranquil beauty of Bali’s coastline. Light refreshments are provided throughout the journey, and guests return to the resort around midday.

Back on shore, the experience continues at Toya Beach Bar & Grill, where the resort’s culinary team transforms the morning’s catch into a bespoke three-course lunch served overlooking the Indian Ocean. Celebrating the freshness of locally sourced seafood, the menu highlights the simple pleasure of enjoying fish prepared just moments after it reaches the shore.

Priced at IDR 4,500,000++ per couple, the package includes the private fishing excursion, refreshments on board, a welcome drink upon arrival, and the three-course lunch. Additional guests can join for IDR 1,500,000++ per person.

Ideal for couples, families or anyone seeking a memorable culinary adventure, Catch & Grill offers a unique way to connect with Bali’s maritime traditions while enjoying one of the island’s most rewarding seafood dining experiences. Departures are subject to daily weather and sea conditions to ensure guest safety.
For more information or reservations, please contact +62 811 3830 5954 or email Sofitel.BaliNusaDua.FBReservation@sofitel.com

title: The Tiger & the Palm-wine Tapper - The Story of I Papaka
dek: The fable of I Papaka, from the Tantra Kamandala tells a moral story. The fable was illustrated as the Tiger and Palm-wine tapper by I Gede..
paras: I Papaka, as illustrated by Kete Gede (c.1890), Collection Van der Tuuk, Leiden University Libraries

We begin this edition (The Drinks Edition) with a fabulous illustration by the Balinese artist I Ketut Gede, titled ‘Fable of the bull, the tiger and the palm-wine tapper’ (c.1890), displaying an early depiction of a Balinese character harvesting ‘tuak’ from a palm tree.

The illustration was commissioned by the Dutch linguist Herman Neubronner van der Tuuk, who lived and worked in the Dutch East Indies, best known for founding the first lontar (Balinese manuscript) library in Singaraja, today known as Gedong Kirtya, North Bali.

A lover of Balinese stories, V.D. Tuuk commissioned I Ketut Gede to create a vast series of Balinese drawings on ink, following the folk stories of I Papaka, the character depicted in the illustration. This particular illustration captures the moment I Papaka, described as a ‘palm wine tapper,’ is attacked by a tiger as he is collecting the ‘tuak’ from the top of a jaka palm tree.

According to Leiden University, the narrative behind this particular scene was that the tiger wanted to prove that he was the highest being on earth by killing man, in this case, I Papaka the palm-wine tapper. Outsmarted, the tiger ends up being tied up to the jaka tree, showing the superiority of man.
Whilst this particular scene sees the tiger as the villain, the wider story turns this around completely.

The I Papala story is one of many fables from the Tantri Kamandaka, a classical story tradition that became deeply established in Bali – akin to the Indian Panchatantra. The Tantri Kamandaka is structured as a chain of interconnected fables, in which stories are told within other stories. At its centre is Diah Tantri, who uses storytelling to teach and ultimately reform the behaviour of King Eswaryadala. The individual tales use animals and humans to illustrate different aspects of human character and morality.

In the original version, it is I Papaka who is shown as the true villain. A cruel hunter, he goes into the forest and shoots at an unsuspecting elephant, who flees into the bush badly injured. The elephant encounters the tiger who complains that such a huge creature shouldn’t be scared of one man, to which the elephant argues it is man’s skill and smarts that makes him dangerous.

The tiger, intent on proving this theory wrong, goes after I Papaka. The fear-stricken hunter attempts to run and is saved by Wanari, a monkey, who helps him up the tree – the Wanari is killed by the tiger. And instead of being grateful, the cruel, cruel hunter then kills the monkey’s two children.
Ultimately, the story was told to draw Papaka as an archetype of total moral failure in a person: he saw the kindness of the monkey as a debt of obligation, leading ultimate betrayal.
Whilst the versions in the image and original story differ (as happens with folk stories!), we nonetheless gifted with a fabulous depiction of the tuak harvest as seen in the 19th century Bali!

title: Savour a Refined Taste of Bali at Raja’s Balinese Cuisine
dek: Raja’s Balinese Cuisine at Nusa Dua Beach Hotel – Handwritten Collection has reopened with a refreshed concept.
paras: Raja’s Balinese Cuisine at Nusa Dua Beach Hotel – Handwritten Collection has reopened with a refreshed concept, presenting a more refined interpretation of Bali’s culinary heritage while staying true to its cultural roots.

The transformation of Raja’s Balinese Cuisine extends beyond the menu, introducing an elegant new interior inspired by traditional Balinese aesthetics. Soft green hues, warm timber finishes, Batik and Patra Bali motifs, hand-carved gebyok doors, and guardian statues create a sophisticated setting that balances tropical warmth with timeless craftsmanship. The restaurant offers guests both indoor and semi-outdoor dining overlooking the resort’s swimming pool.

Meaning “king” in Indonesian, Raja’s embraces the idea of a royal dining experience through a contemporary take on authentic Balinese cuisine. Here, traditional recipes from across the island are thoughtfully reimagined using modern techniques while preserving their distinctive regional flavours.

Among the highlights is Segaran lan Gunung, a slow-braised beef brisket served with velvety butternut purée, rich bumbu semur, and the restaurant’s fragrant sambal bongkot. Named after Bali’s symbolic connection between the sea (segara) and mountains (gunung), the dish celebrates the harmony of the island’s landscapes and culinary traditions.

The menu also showcases regional favourites, including Tipat Blayag Singaraja, Lawar Plek Ulam Banteng from Gianyar, Bebek Suna Cekuh from Nusa Dua, and Kuah Rambanan from Negara. To finish, guests can sample a selection of traditional Balinese jaje, offering a fitting introduction to the island’s beloved sweet treats. Seamlessly blending heritage-inspired design with elevated local cuisine, Raja’s new chapter promises a fresh way to experience the richness and diversity of Balinese gastronomy.
For more information or reservations, please contact +62 811 3820 5649 or email fbreservations@nusaduahotel.com

title: Alaya Suites Ubud Opens in the Heart of Pengosekan
dek: Alaya Suites Ubud brings together contemporary design, Balinese storytelling and personalised Indonesian hospitality in an intimate setting.
paras: Ubud welcomes a new boutique hospitality destination with the opening of Alaya Suites Ubud, the latest addition to the Alaya Hotels & Resorts portfolio. Located in Pengosekan, the new property brings together contemporary design, Balinese storytelling and personalised Indonesian hospitality in an intimate setting.

Designed around the “Dream of Alaya” concept, the property takes inspiration from Catus Patha, the traditional Balinese principle centred on the intersection of community, ritual and daily life. Its architecture also draws from Wayang Bali, with curved forms, natural textures and organic materials woven throughout the space. Each floor reflects one of the five natural elements: Surya (light), Bhumi (earth), Sagara (water), Jiva (living beings) and Akasha (air).

Alaya Suites Ubud comprises 45 spacious suites and six private villas, making it one of the few properties in central Ubud dedicated exclusively to suites and villas. Handcrafted details, locally sourced materials and Indonesian design touches feature throughout, complemented by amenities including eco-friendly slippers, handcrafted tote bags and kimonos by Indonesian lifestyle brand Pithecanthropus.

Dining takes centre stage with Carbón, which explores the bold, fire-led flavours of Mexico and Peru, while Baker Butcher Barista transitions from specialty coffee, pastries and breads by day to a steakhouse experience by evening. DaLa Spa brings Indonesian wellness traditions into the stay, complemented by a fully equipped TechnoGym fitness centre.

With its thoughtful design, intimate accommodation and strong sense of place, Alaya Suites Ubud offers travellers a considered way to experience the energy and creativity of Ubud while staying connected to the island’s cultural character.
For more information or reservations, please contact +62 361 201 3808 or follow @alaya.suites

title: Discover The Alchemist’s Spice Route at L’Atelier by Cyril Kongo
dek: At the top of The Apurva Kempinski Bali, where art, craftsmanship and indulgence come together, L’Atelier by Cyril Kongo is entering a new chapter. For 2026, the…
paras: At the top of The Apurva Kempinski Bali, where art, craftsmanship and indulgence come together, L’Atelier by Cyril Kongo is entering a new chapter. For 2026, the avant-garde studio and lifestyle destination introduces Spice Route Creative, a cocktail programme that looks beyond the glass to explore Indonesia’s long and complex relationship with spice.

Since opening in 2021, the 144-square-metre L’Atelier has occupied a distinctive space within the resort, doubling as a working art studio and an intimate lounge for cigars, champagne, wine and spirits. Created in collaboration with French-Vietnamese graffiti artist Cyril Kongo, whose work has been commissioned by international houses including Hermès, Chanel and Richard Mille, the venue has always blurred the lines between art and lifestyle.

The premise is simple: spice is identity. Long before it became a defining ingredient in Indonesian cuisine, the archipelago’s spices were precious commodities that shaped trade, wealth, power and even conquest. Through the new menu, L’Atelier brings this history into a contemporary setting, using local ingredients as a way to tell stories of nature, heritage and culture.

Each of the nine cocktails centres on a spice indigenous to the Indonesian archipelago, while three pillars provide the programme’s narrative foundation. Nature draws attention to Bali’s landscapes and the importance of preserving them. Heritage celebrates traditional crafts and the people working to keep them alive. Culture uncovers lesser-known stories, techniques and meanings behind Indonesia’s local traditions.

The philosophy continues through three guiding principles: craftsmanship, refinement and tradition. Techniques are used to reinterpret familiar flavours, presentations are deliberately modern, and every cocktail is designed to arrive with a story and a sense of purpose.

At the centre of this new programme is Arya, known behind the bar as “The Alchemist”. A Bali-born mixologist with deep connections to the island’s traditions, Arya serves as Bar Manager at L’Atelier, where he channels local knowledge into contemporary creations. For this edition, he has placed particular emphasis on Arak Bali, the traditional palm- or rice-based spirit, creating a series of experiences that present the archipelago’s oldest spirit through a fresh perspective.

Arya’s approach is also grounded in responsibility. His commitment to local farmers, producers and sustainable practices was recognised when he was crowned the Indonesia Regional Winner of the Hennessy MyWay 2025 competition, earning the opportunity to represent Indonesia at the global finals in France. At L’Atelier, he continues to champion local artistry while encouraging his team to create drinks that feel both distinctly Balinese and internationally relevant.

Two cocktails offer a glimpse into this philosophy. Varun, under the Culture pillar, takes inspiration from the Indian Ocean and the coastal landscapes of southern Bali. Combining vodka, Karu18, white cardamom, algae and oregano in a contemporary twist on the Blue Lagoon, the cocktail is connected to a coral and ocean-life preservation programme supporting local fishermen, developed with the Living Seas Foundation and Coral Sense Bali.

Then there is Battle Ritual, a drink rooted in one of Bali’s most compelling traditions. Inspired by Perang Pandan, the ritual combat practised by the Bali Aga community in Tenganan in Karangasem, the cocktail reflects a ceremony associated with bravery, confidence and emotional discipline. East Indies Gin meets pandan, vetiver, longan and honey in a reinterpretation of the Bee’s Knees, while the drink supports a pandan seedling-planting programme in Desa Tenganan, developed with Samsara Living and the Tenganan community.

For Arya, the purpose is not to reinvent these traditions, but to translate them. As he explains, each cocktail begins with a story already present in Bali – a ritual, ceremony, or tradition passed down through generations. The bartender’s role, then, is to make that story accessible to a global audience without losing its authenticity.

This is perhaps what makes Spice Route Creative more than a new cocktail menu. At L’Atelier by Cyril Kongo, the spice becomes a medium for storytelling: connecting the land to the glass, the past to the present, and Bali’s living traditions to a new generation of curious drinkers.

title: Carbón Brings Latin American Fire to Ubud
dek: From Jakarta to Bali, Carbón Ubud brings Latin American-inspired flavours to the island as they open within Alaya Suites Ubud.
paras: Following its success in Jakarta, Carbón has opened its doors in Ubud, introducing a more intimate interpretation of its Latin American-inspired dining concept. Located within the newly opened Alaya Suites Ubud on Jalan Raya Pengosekan, the restaurant is the result of a collaboration between MDA Restaurants and Alaya Group, marking the brand’s first venture into Bali.

Rather than replicating its Jakarta counterpart, the restaurant has been thoughtfully adapted to its surroundings. While retaining the brand’s signature fire-led cooking, the menu embraces the abundance of Bali’s seasonal produce, drawing on natural affinities between Mexican, Peruvian and Indonesian cuisine. Ingredients such as chilli, corn, cacao, tropical fruits and fresh herbs create a menu that feels rooted in Latin America whilst reflecting Ubud’s rich agricultural landscape.

Leading the kitchen is Chef Patron Andri Dionysius, whose philosophy remains centred on quality ingredients and restrained technique. Alongside an à la carte selection featuring Carbón favourites and Ubud-exclusive creations, guests can embark on a thoughtfully curated tasting menu, designed as an evolving culinary journey with future editions set to showcase new seasonal inspirations. A well-rounded beverage programme complements the experience with classic cocktails, wines and carefully crafted non-alcoholic pairings.

Warm, intimate interiors complete the experience, offering a refined yet relaxed setting suited to long lunches, romantic dinners or celebratory evenings. As Ubud’s culinary landscape continues to evolve, Carbón Ubud adds a distinctive new destination where Latin American flavours meet the spirit of Bali.
For more information or reservations, please contact +62 851 8394 2923 or follow @carbon.ubud

title: KU DE TA Boutique Brings Curated Island Fashion to Seminyak
dek: KU DE TA Boutique is a refined retail space celebrating island fashion, artisan craftsmanship and contemporary resort style.
paras: Seminyak’s beachfront lifestyle destination, KU DE TA, has expanded its offering with the opening of KU DE TA Boutique, a refined retail space celebrating island fashion, artisan craftsmanship and contemporary resort style.

Open daily from 12pm to 9pm, KU DE TA Boutique brings together a curated selection of women’s and men’s resort wear, statement dresses, swimwear, jewellery and handcrafted accessories. Designed with KU DE TA’s effortless coastal aesthetic in mind, the space offers an easy transition from a day by the sea to an afternoon of leisurely shopping.

The collection features a mix of regional and international labels, each bringing its own interpretation of modern island dressing. Highlights include the ocean-inspired silhouettes of Mauricio Alpizar, the bohemian elegance of Erika Peña and SONN’s minimalist designs for tropical living. Religion adds an edgier touch, while ‘Til T’morrow and Inna The Brand offer versatile pieces suited to both daytime and evening. Indonesian craftsmanship is represented by Momo Batik, which reinterprets traditional textiles through a contemporary lens.

“The opening of the boutique allows us to offer a complete lifestyle experience. Guests can now immerse themselves in our unique aesthetic and take home exceptional, curated fashion that captures the true essence of Bali,” says Matthew Spice, General Manager of KU DE TA.

Additionally, the boutique also offers personalised styling through WhatsApp, allowing guests to arrange private sessions, preview new arrivals and organise tailored fittings during their stay in Bali.
For more information, please contact +62 361 736969 or WhatsApp the Personal Style Advisor at +62 813 9801 503.

title: Merasa Origins: Tracing Java’s Ancient Wellness Traditions at Desa Potato Head
dek: Desa Potato Head continues its Merasa Origins series with its second chapter, Java: Entering Depth, taking place from 10-13 September 2026.
paras: Following the success of its inaugural chapter, India: Beginning with Balance with Reema Datta, Desa Potato Head is continuing its Merasa Origins series this September with its second chapter, Java: Entering Depth, taking place from 10-13 September 2026.

A three-part exploration of the cultural roots behind Bali’s wellness traditions, Merasa Origins traces a historical journey from India to Java and, ultimately, Bali. Across three four-day immersions, the series brings together practitioners and cultural voices to explore how philosophy, ritual and physical practice have travelled across generations and evolved through different places.

At the heart of the programme is merasa, the Indonesian word for “to feel”. At Desa Potato Head, this philosophy is reflected in an approach to well-being that is experienced rather than prescribed, bringing together movement, meditation, breathwork, traditional therapies, plant-based healing and sound practices.

The Java chapter turns its attention to the introspective traditions of ancient Jawadwipa. Guided by Tantric priest Pak Sugeng and spiritual anthropologist Serj Hunt, the four-day programme draws from Hindu-Buddhist Tantra and Javanese Kebatinan, exploring teachings and rituals passed down through sacred lineages.

Participants will move through morning practices, Javanese dance, collective mantras and workshops exploring Tattwa Tutur, the three forms of Broto and the principles of Right Relationship. Rituals including Yadnya, Upacara and a Tolak Balak ceremony offer deeper insight into Javanese approaches to devotion, protection and spiritual balance.

Rather than presenting these traditions as isolated techniques, Merasa Origins invites participants to experience them as interconnected systems shaped by history, place and community. The journey will conclude in Bali this November, completing the series and returning to the island where these layered traditions continue to shape contemporary approaches to well-being.
For more information, contact +62 361 620 7979, follow @potatoheadbali on Instagram, or visit seminyak.potatohead.co/merasa-origins.

title: Bali Gapura Marina Expands Indonesia’s Luxury Maritime Gateway
dek: Bali Gapura Marina has marked another milestone in its development as Indonesia’s first international superyacht gateway.
paras: Bali Gapura Marina has marked another milestone in its development as Indonesia’s first international superyacht gateway with the inauguration of its new Welcome Station and Dock C.

Held on 16 July 2026, the occasion also saw the launch of the Bali Gapura Marina Ocean Challenge 2026 and a series of strategic partnerships aimed at strengthening Bali’s position on the global luxury yachting map.

The new Welcome Station serves as the first point of arrival for international yacht owners and guests, bringing together Customs, Immigration, Quarantine and Port Clearance (CIQP) services with premium hospitality and streamlined arrival procedures. Designed and built by 2M Associate, the facility reflects the marina’s vision of combining efficient infrastructure with a more seamless guest experience.

Among the event’s key announcements was a new partnership with Fly Odisi, making Bali Gapura Marina its official seaplane berthing location and passenger embarkation and disembarkation hub. The collaboration creates an integrated air-and-sea gateway, connecting travellers with superyachts and destinations across Indonesia.

Further partnerships with Pacific High Group and Luxe Horizon, SEABOB, Vedanta, Vivre and Lago Resort Nusa Lembongan will expand the marina’s offering through bespoke travel experiences, marine recreation, yacht charters, culinary services and curated island escapes.

The inauguration culminated in the Bali Gapura Marina Ocean Challenge, a flotilla sailing from the marina to Lago Resort, Nusa Lembongan. Against Bali’s coastline, the experience showcased how yachting, hospitality and island exploration can come together, offering a glimpse of the island’s evolving role in Southeast Asia’s luxury maritime landscape.

title: Art Takes Centre Stage at BK Creative Hub
dek: BK Creative Hub is a creative space where contemporary art, creativity, wellness and human connection come together under one roof.
paras: Seminyak has welcomed a new creative destination with the opening of BK Creative Hub, a creative space where contemporary art, creativity, wellness and human connection come together under one roof.

Officially launched on 19 June 2026, BK Creative Hub was founded by Alexa Genoyer, an entrepreneur, artist, and hotelier behind Blue Karma’s boutique properties in Bali. Drawing from her belief that creativity can reconnect people with themselves, each other, and culture, the new space marks the physical evolution of her global digital platform, Lucid Dream Art.

At its heart is a 500-square-metre exhibition space featuring The Cube 1 and The Cube 2, complemented by interactive workshop studios, Sensual Clay and Sensory experiences, as well as an Art Café where food and colour become part of the creative experience.

The opening also marked the debut of Ade Habibie’s solo exhibition, Monkey Spirit. Featuring 35 original works across the gallery’s two exhibition cubes, the collection uses the monkey as a playful symbol through which to explore human emotion, instinct, and vulnerability.

BK Creative Hub invites visitors to experience art through participation, discovery, and connection. As Alexa puts it, the hub is created “for everyone – not only those who collect art, but those who want to experience creativity.”
Monkey Spirit is currently open to the public, offering visitors and art connoisseurs an opportunity to explore the exhibition and discover Seminyak’s newest creative hub.
For more information, please contact +62 813 383 8910 or follow @bluekarmacreativehub

title: New Restaurants in Bali 2026: Latest Openings [Updated]
dek: Looking for new restaurants in Bali or the hottest new bar opened in 2026? Look no further, our monthly updated list is your go-to guide.
paras: The island’s world-class food and beverage scene continues to grow and innovate, adding to the already fantastic variety of venues in which to eat, drink and enjoy. Brand new venues – be it a late-night speakeasy, the latest fine-dining destination or a comfy new café – are still popping up across Bali, and here we bring you some of the most notable new kids in town. So, if you’re looking for the best new restaurants in Bali in 2026 or the most intriguing new bar, don’t look any further.
We’ll be updating this article every month, so make sure to subscribe to our newsletter to stay in the loop!

Designed around ‘An Evening in Seven Chapters’, RISERVA is the latest addition to The Wonderspace portfolio, bringing premium steaks, fine wines and Balinese-inspired rituals to Ubud. Set within Equipoise Resort, the intimate steakhouse welcomes just 16 guests per evening for a carefully paced dining experience.

The evening begins at sunset with a series of arrival rituals, from the Gong Ritual and Foot Wash Ritual to Seven Tirta and Final Purification. Guests then enjoy a personalised Wariga experience, followed by welcome canapés, or Lungsuran, and a welcome drink. A ceremonial Champagne Sabrage marks the transition to dinner.

At the heart of the experience is Chef Putu Armen’s menu, which celebrates premium ingredients and a selection of wagyu cuts, allowing diners to appreciate the distinct texture and richness of each. The steak course is accompanied by two signature rituals: Seven Knives, inspired by Bali’s pande tradition of master metal artisans, and Seven Salts, featuring artisanal salts from Bali and around the world, including Tejakula salt from North Bali.

The wine programme, curated by Bali Best Sommelier 2025, I Putu Erawan Ari Widhiantika, spans renowned regions across Europe, the Americas, Oceania and South Africa. A Coravin programme also offers a wider selection by the glass. The evening continues at Aura Lounge, where petit desserts and crafted cocktails invite guests to linger over the valley views.
RISERVA welcomes both resort guests and visitors. With one seating each night, reservations are essential.

Petitenget’s dining scene welcomes a new address for classic American steakhouse fare with the arrival of Wolfgang’s Steakhouse, the Manhattan-born restaurant celebrated for dry-aged USDA Prime beef, polished service and old-school New York hospitality.

Officially opened on 21 August 2026 at Parc Valle Petitenget, the Bali outpost marks another chapter in the brand’s Indonesian expansion, following its first Jakarta restaurant in 2020. Its arrival brings a distinctly Manhattan character to one of Bali’s busiest dining neighbourhoods, with warm mahogany panelling, patterned tiles and soft ambient lighting creating a timeless setting.

At the heart of the experience is USDA Prime beef, dry-aged for 28 days under carefully monitored temperature and humidity. Among the signatures is the Porterhouse, combining tender Filet Mignon and rich New York Strip in one substantial cut. Chef Amiro Cruz explains that the steak is broiled at an intense temperature to create a deeply caramelised crust while preserving its natural juices and tenderness.

Presented sliced on a sizzling platter with bone intact, the Porterhouse captures the restaurant’s approach to dining: premium ingredients, precise technique and a sense of occasion. A dedicated cocktail programme complements the menu, alongside attentive service synonymous with the brand.

With locations across the US and Asia, Wolfgang’s Steakhouse has established a global following while maintaining its Manhattan roots. In Bali, it offers a refined setting for a classic steak dinner, cocktails and celebrations, bringing a taste of old-school New York to Petitenget.

title: The Westin Resort Nusa Dua, Bali Presents Celebrate Wellness 2026
dek: Wellness takes centre stage at Celebrate Wellness 2026, a full-day experience designed to inspire a more balanced approach to healthy living.
paras: On Saturday, 12 September 2026, wellness takes centre stage at Celebrate Wellness 2026, a full-day experience designed to inspire a more balanced approach to healthy living. Bringing together movement, nutrition, holistic health and expert insights, the event invites guests to explore wellness in ways that feel both practical and personal.

Taking place at the Bali International Convention Center, The Westin Resort Nusa Dua, Bali, Celebrate Wellness 2026 features Pilates, Vinyasa yoga, fitness sessions and thought-provoking wellness talks, alongside a healthy lunch and access to the Vibrant Bazaar, where guests can discover a curated selection of health and wellness brands.

Hosted by wellness personality Mika Affandy, the day brings together an inspiring line-up of experts including Kris Abbey, founder of Spa & Wellness Australia; Dr. Jitendra Pokhriyal, Director of Wellness at The Westin Resort Nusa Dua, Bali; wellness personalities Ganindra Bimo and Andrea Dian; Pilates instructors Gung Iss and Cok Shara of Manawa Studios Bali; and yoga personality Fangtatis of Active Barn Jakarta.

The day begins with Pilates on the Mat led by Gung Iss and Cok Shara (9am – 10am), followed by a Vinyasa Yoga session with Fangtatis (10:30am – 12pm). After a healthy lunch prepared by Dr. Jitendra Pokhriyal and Chef Raviel Sidik (12:30pm – 2pm), guests can join a wellness talk with Kris Abbey and Dr. Jitendra (2:30pm – 3:30pm) before wrapping up the afternoon with an energetic workout led by Andrea Dian and Ganindra Bimo (4pm – 5pm). A closing session with all wellness experts brings the day to a close.

Beyond the sessions, tickets include an exclusive Adidas jersey, a Sensatia goodie bag, a healthy lunch, full access to the wellness programme, entry to the Vibrant Bazaar and the chance to win a selection of door prizes.
Registration starts at 7am, while the event kicks off at 9am until 5.30pm. The ticket is priced at IDR 500,000 per person and can be purchased via Tiket.com.
For more information, visit westinnusaduabali.com or follow @WestinBali on Instagram.

title: Discover Ancient Rituals and Modern Healing Journeys in Bali
dek: Discover Bali wellness experiences from sacred purification rituals and traditional healing to wellness retreats and regenerative biohacking.
paras: Bali has evolved into one of the world’s leading wellness destinations, where ancient healing traditions exist alongside modern wellness innovations. From sacred purification rituals and traditional healing to sound therapy, slow wellness retreats and regenerative biohacking, the island offers a diverse range of experiences that nurture mind, body and spirit. Together, they reflect Bali’s enduring healing culture and its evolution into a globally recognised centre for holistic well-being.

Among Bali’s most enduring spiritual traditions is melukat, a sacred purification ritual rooted in Balinese Hindu belief. Performed using tirta (holy water) sourced from natural springs, rivers, waterfalls or the sea, the ceremony is intended to cleanse the mind, body and soul of negative influences, restoring balance and harmony within oneself. Led by a pemangku (Balinese priest), participants move through a series of prayers and blessings before bathing in sacred waters, embracing a practice that’s been passed down through generations as a means of spiritual renewal.

There are several notable sites across the island where melukat rituals are conducted, including Tirta Empul Temple, Campuhan Windhu Segara Temple, Mengening Temple, Tirta Sudamala Temple and Taman Beji Griya Waterfall. Each location follows its own purification process, with a specific sequence of fountains, pools or waterfalls that you’ll move through during the ritual. Beyond the ceremony itself, every site encapsulates a distinct atmosphere, from temple courtyards steeped in history to secluded natural springs hidden within lush landscapes.

For those seeking a more serene and immersive experience, Gunung Kawi Sebatu Temple offers a quieter alternative. Surrounded by forested valleys and fed by sacred springs believed to have healing properties, the temple and its nearby purification sites invite visitors into a setting where nature and spirituality intertwine. Away from the crowds, the journey through moss-covered shrines, flowing waters and tranquil surroundings becomes as meaningful as the ritual itself, offering a deeper sense of reflection, connection and renewal.

For centuries, yoga has offered a pathway to physical vitality, mental clarity and inner balance. At Prana Spa in Seminyak, this ancient practice unfolds in a serene setting inspired by the grandeur of Indian and Middle Eastern architecture, fostering an atmosphere of mindfulness and restoration.

Designed for practitioners of all levels, yoga at Prana focuses on the harmonious connection between movement, breath and awareness. Guided sessions combine gentle postures, stretching, and breathing techniques to improve flexibility, strength, and balance while encouraging participants to slow down and reconnect with themselves.

Beyond its physical benefits, yoga remains a powerful tool for managing stress and cultivating a sense of calm amidst the pace of modern life. The tranquil surroundings of the studio further enhance the experience, offering a dedicated space for reflection and renewal in the heart of Seminyak. Whether joining a regular class, attending a workshop or participating in a wellness retreat, guests are invited to embrace a practice that has supported well-being for thousands of years.

Across cultures and centuries, sound has been used as a tool for mediation, healing and spiritual connection. At Taru Pramana Wellness & Spa within The Meru Sanur, this ancient practice is reimagined through an immersive sound healing experience inspired by Bali’s rich healing traditions.

Rooted in the philosophy of Lontar Buda Kecapi – one of Bali’s revered healing manuscripts – the experience embraces the belief that well-being is achieved when the body, mind and spirit exist in harmony. Each session begins with a deeper exploration of the individual, drawing from traditional Balinese approaches to understanding personal balance and well-being.

Guests are then guided into a meditative state through carefully curated sounds and vibrations designed to encourage relaxation and self-awareness. The resonant frequencies help quiet the mind, ease physical tension and create a sense of inner stillness, allowing them to reconnect with themselves on a deeper level.

Blending ancestral wisdom with contemporary wellness practices, the sound healing at The Meru Sanur presents a restorative journey that extends beyond relaxation. It is an opportunity to pause, listen and experience the therapeutic power of sound in a setting dedicated to holistic well-being and renewal.

As wellness continues to evolve, many travellers are shifting away from intensive programmes and packed itineraries in favour of a more mindful approach known as slow wellness. Rooted in the principles of slow travel, the philosophy encourages rest, reflection and profound connection, prioritising presence over productivity and experience over achievement.

title: Artist Agung Pramana Questions Colonial Propaganda Narratives & Imagery
dek: Blending printmaking traditions with experimental modern ideas, Agung Pramana offers a vibrant, accessible view of Bali's cultural heritage.
paras: Three hundred and thirty-six blue and white cyanotype prints, 20 by 15cm, arranged floor to ceiling within a 6-meter-deep by 5-meter-wide alcove of the Jogja National Museum (JNM), distinguish *After Exotic 1931*, a contemporary art installation by Balinese printmaker Agung Pramana.

Immediately captivating, Pramana’s visual formula pulsates. Reproduction archival images, Balinese sculptures of mythical creatures, Hindu Gods, and human figures, are layered on horizontal and vertical measurement grids, characteristic of technical documentation. The repetitive imagery is a simplified Pop Art formula of white designs on a deep blue background, intentionally blurred to create ambiguous meaning, allowing for reinterpretation.

*After Exotic 1931* on display at Indonesia’s premier contemporary art festival, ARTJOG 2026 ARS LONGA: GENERATIO, from 19 July – 31 August 2026 at JNM, references the 1931 Paris Colonial Exhibition. During an era of imperial global conquest, the pioneering international showcase of colonial plunder was instrumental in shaping Western views of non-European cultures like Bali. From the 1850s onwards, colonial officials and missionaries collected Balinese artefacts for European museums, including Amsterdam's Tropenmuseum.

Traversing new aesthetic territory, Agung Pramana introduces a fresh contemporary art language by adopting the cyanotype printing technique and making an historical association with colonial practices employed for construction blueprints and archaeological records throughout colonial territories. Discovered in 1842, cyanotype is a slow-reacting printing formulation sensitive to a limited near-ultraviolet and blue light spectrum.

Pramana’s cyanotype process creates blue images by placing objects on paper coated with a light-sensitive solution of iron salts and exposing it to a UV lamp machine to keep the colour intensity consistent. The areas exposed to light turn blue, while the areas covered by the objects remain white, resulting in a striking contrast known as Prussian Blue.

“My interest in colonialism grew after the beginning of the Russia-Ukraine war, which escalated into a full-scale invasion by Russia in early 2022 and witnessing many Russians, Ukrainians and other nationalities settle in Southeast Asia, especially Bali. I then contemplated the relationship between tourists and local communities, and the impact of mass tourism,” Agung Pramana told NOW!Bali Magazine. “I realised the issue isn't just about tourists; it's also about corrupt officials and weak regulations, and the attitude of the Balinese people.”

“I then researched colonialism, post-colonialism, and de-colonialism; reading from diverse perspectives deepening my interest in historical issues: their origins, how knowledge systems evolve, and how we might re-examine that history today,” said Pramana, born in 1998 in Jembarna, West Bali, whose solo exhibition Print-Mapping: Decolonial Axis at SIKA Gallery in Ubud was open throughout January 2026.

“I sourced images of Balinese sculptures and reliefs from European museums, then reworked them into critical, confrontational art pieces. One of my early works depicts a curved keris (ceremonial dagger) piercing its holder, symbolising how power and relationships can harm both sides—what we use for protection can also become a threat. The series, “Looting Back,” evolved into my exhibition, “Print-Mapping: Decolonial Axis.”

“Yet I then became trapped in a cycle of anger and anxiety—mainly about copyright, image sources, and the possibility of my work being misinterpreted. This added to my distress, so I shifted my research focus more toward historical aspects,” said Pramana, who is one of the team at DEVFTO Printmaking Institute, located at SIKA Gallery, Ubud.
After Exotic 1931 - Agung Pramana ARTJOG 2026 ARS LONGA_ GENERATIO. Image Agung Pramana.

“I examined the original catalogue from the 1931 Paris Colonial Exposition, learning that the Dutch brought Balinese sculptures and artefacts to Paris, displaying them as exotic objects, aiming to present the administration as a humanist power that introduced colonial cultures to Europe. This made me rethink decolonisation and how Eastern societies have been portrayed. Too often, we are seen as objects—defined and labelled by others—instead of as self-defining sovereign subjects.”

“I addressed this issue by replicating colonial systems of mapping, documentation, archiving, and classification from my Eastern perspective. Using their visual language and methods, I reconstructed "exoticism" from a new vantage point,” Pramana stated. “I used cyanotype, historically tied to reproducing blueprints and technical documents. My aim was to invert the colonial gaze—shifting from how the West mapped the East to how I, as part of the East, remap that history and the idea of exoticism.”

title: A Moon on Water: How Two Design Teams, A Sea Apart, Shaped the Building of SAKA
dek: The director of SAKA Museum traces how architects & interior designers turned the spirit of Nyepi into a world-renowned beautiful museum.
paras: At dusk, the great roof settles into an upturned crescent — a moon on water, mirrored in the surrounding pool. Photography: Mario Wibowo.

Tucked inside AYANA Bali, SAKA Museum takes the shape of a moon on still water. Here its director traces how the building’s architects and its interior designers turned the spirit of Nyepi — Bali’s Day of Silence — into a museum now counted among the most beautiful in the world.

Descend the long walkway that leads down into SAKA, and something happens to the light. The Balinese sun — that great, generous presence everywhere else in the resort — falls away behind you. The ceiling lowers, the air cools, and you arrive in a darkened hall scattered with points of light, hovering over a still sheet of water. Visitors slow almost without noticing. They have stepped, quite deliberately, into another register: quiet, submerged, expectant.

That threshold is no accident. It is the meeting point of two conversations about what this building should be — one with a Japanese firm, the other with a Hong Kong studio — and the story of SAKA’s design is really the story of how they came to say the same thing.

The museum’s structure was designed by the Japanese firm Mitsubishi Jisho Design (MJD), whose Global Design Office handles projects across Asia. Its lead designer, Haruka Sato, shaped the concept; senior advisor Yosuke Takahashi, who spent decades at the firm before taking charge of its overseas projects some fifteen years ago, oversaw its realisation as project supervisor. What began years ago as a brief for a shopping and cultural precinct near AYANA’s cliffside Rock Bar slowly deepened — through on-site workshops and long conversations with the owners — into something with a museum at its heart.

That it became a museum at all owed most to the owner’s own preoccupation. For years he had wanted to show visitors “the truth of Nyepi” (the Balinese Day of Silence that marks the Saka New Year) — a day, he notes, that most tourists never see, when the island falls dark and silent and the sky fills with stars, and whose eve brings the parade of ogoh-ogoh (towering effigies of demons and spirits). SAKA was conceived to carry that experience to the world.
From the side, the roof sweeps to a single point at the water's edge, glowing against the last light. Photography: Mario Wibowo.

Sato’s guiding idea was “A Moon on Water.” She had been struck by a traditional Indonesian verse — “only in still water can the true image of the moon be seen” — and set out to give that stillness a form. “I wanted this building to symbolise quiet introspection,” she says: a place to pause, to look inward. The great sloping roof carries the idea into form, reading as a crescent moon — but not the upright crescent familiar in Europe. “In countries near the equator, such as Indonesia, the crescent moon sometimes appears with its tips pointing upward. I wanted to capture that curved shape in the design.” It is a sight caught best low on the horizon at dusk.

She gave that curve a precise geometry, a catenary (the curve a chain settles into when it hangs freely under its own weight, fixed at both ends) — a shape found by gravity rather than imposed by the hand, and one that also recalls the broad, sweeping roofs of traditional Indonesian architecture. The museum’s very name keeps the moon in view: SAKA takes it from the Balinese Saka lunisolar calendar, which has ordered daily life on the island for centuries.

Later, others would find further meanings in the form — a line drawn between mountain and sea, even a compass laid across the plan, its arms pointing to the cardinal directions so important in Balinese cosmology. Those readings were not the architects’ intention, and they delight in them all the same. What Sato did insist upon was orientation: the building turns to face the sunset, its long façades set east and west, shielding the interior from the tropical heat while framing the light.
By day, framed by bougainvillea; the long façades set east–west, turned towards the sunset. Photography: Mario Wibowo.

Water runs through the design as both symbol and substance. Sato drew on Tri Hita Karana (the Balinese philosophy of harmony between nature, humankind and the divine), in which the water cycle — expressed in Bali’s ancient subak (communal irrigation system) — stands for abundance. Water became a connecting thread, linking building, spirit and people; a cascade was set to run along the slope.

title: ORYn Brings Smoke, Spice & Spirits to the Ubud Culinary Landscape
dek: Opened in June, ORYn brings together an open-fire kitchen, bold flavours & imaginative sips under 3 defining pillars: Smoke, Spice & Spirits.
paras: Opened in June 2026, ORYn brings together an open-fire kitchen, bold flavours, and imaginative sips under three defining pillars: Smoke, Spice, and Spirits. Founded by hospitality entrepreneurs Tom and Bina Philip, the team behind The Blue Door, ORYn offers an upscale-casual setting in central Ubud that accomodates up to 75 guests.

At the helm is Head Chef Danial Fitri Yap, whose culinary background includes Michelin-starred kitchens in Singapore and a stint as Head Chef at CÉ LA VI atop Marina Bay Sands. At ORYn, his experience is channelled into what the restaurant describes as “raw refinement”, a cooking philosophy that pairs the natural character of quality ingredients with considered technique, with fire serving as the central tool.

ORYn's menu is designed around sharing, moving freely across culinary traditions rather than being tied to one particular cuisine. Fresh seafood meets a cool yet lively heat with dishes like kingfish ceviche served with green chilli coconut vinaigrette, while the steak programme places premium, highly marbled cuts over the flames, culminating in the signature tomahawk. The open-fire approach is more pronounced in offerings of charred cabbage, tiger prawns, black cod and house-made pulled noodles.

The restaurant's philosophy extends into the bar, where the drinks programme is another expression of Smoke, Spice and Spirits rather than just accompaniment to the food. The cocktail menu draws on gin, rum and agave, for their natural affinity with heat and smoke. Mirasol tinctures, falernum, torch ginger, palo santo, masoyi and coffee wood introduce aromatic and botanical layers to the drinks.

"Fire gives ingredients depth and character, while spice and acidity bring energy and balance. We focus on clarity of flavour — respecting the ingredient while pushing it just enough to make it memorable. The result is food that feels vibrant, expressive, and made to be shared," said Chef Danial.

For Tom and Bina Philip, the concept is ultimately about more than culinary technique. "At ORYn, we are returning to the origins of flavour," they explain, describing the restaurant as a meeting point between the raw beauty of the earth and the transformative power of the hearth.

"We've created a space where unrefined ingredients meet refined technique — an earthy, immersive experience where every dish feels pulled directly from the elements. Beyond the craft, ORYn is about the alchemy of the moment: the dim glow of the fire, the weight of a glass in hand, and the effortless transition from a dinner to a memory."

title: Wolfgang’s Steakhouse Launches in Petitenget with Classic New York Dining
dek: Petitenget’s dining scene has welcomed a new address for lovers of classic American steakhouse fare with Wolfgang’s Steakhouse Bali.
paras: Petitenget’s dining scene has welcomed a new address for lovers of classic American steakhouse fare with Wolfgang’s Steakhouse, the celebrated Manhattan-born restaurant known for its dry-aged USDA Prime beef and old-school New York hospitality.

Officially opened on 21 August 2026, the Bali outpost marks a long-awaited expansion for the brand, which first entered Indonesia in 2020. Located within Parc Valle Petitenget, Wolfgang’s Steakhouse's arrival adds a distinctly Manhattan character to one of Bali’s most prominent dining neighbourhoods, combining premium steaks, polished service and a timeless interior.

Rather than leaning into Bali’s predominantly seafood and relaxed dining aesthetic, the restaurant deliberately embraces its New York fine dining identity to distinguish itself in the island’s luxury dining landscape. The warm mahogany wood panelling, patterned tiles and soft ambient lighting are complemented by a dedicated cocktail programme and signature attentive service.

At the centre of the Wolfgang’s experience is its USDA Prime beef, which undergoes a 28-day dry-ageing process wherein temperature and humidity are closely monitored. One of the signature dishes is the Porterhouse, a substantial T-bone steak separating two distinct cuts: the tender Filet Mignon and the rich New York Strip, as explained by Chef Amiro Cruz.

The steak is broiled at an extremely high temperature to develop a deeply caramelised exterior while retaining the meat's natural juices and tenderness. The steak is then sliced and presented on a sizzling platter, with the bone remaining part of the presentation. It is a style of service that reflects Wolfgang’s philosophy: premium ingredients, precise technique and a sense of occasion.

Wolfgang’s Steakhouse has grown from its Manhattan roots into an international restaurant group with locations across the US and Asia. Indonesia has become an increasingly important part of that endeavour, with the Bali restaurant following the brand’s first one in Jakarta at ÉLYSÉE SCBD and Wolfgang’s Teppan at Keraton at The Plaza.

"Bali is an important part of our expansion journey, and we see our presence here as an opportunity to bring the authentic New York steakhouse experience to the local community as well as visitors from around the world," said Peter Zwiener, a founder of Wolfgang’s Steakhouse. Another founder, Lydia D’Amato, added, "Through the opening of Wolfgang’s Steakhouse Bali, we are committed to introducing one of Wolfgang’s signature concepts, dry-aging, while delivering a steak experience defined by the quality and character that have become synonymous with our brand."

In line with this, Rudy Salim, CEO of Prestige Corp and Shareholder Partner of Wolfgang’s Steakhouse & Wolfgang Teppan Indonesia, shared his optimism about Bali’s evolving luxury culinary landscape: "This partnership reflects our belief that the combination of Wolfgang’s Steakhouse’s global reputation and Petitenget’s unique appeal will make the restaurant a new must-visit destination for anyone coming to Bali," he explained.

Now open to the public, Wolfgang’s Steakhouse Bali offers another reason to make Petitenget a destination for a special dinner. Whether for a classic Porterhouse, an intimate celebration or simply an evening of steak and cocktails, the new restaurant brings a taste of old-school Manhattan dining to Bali.

title: Where the Next Generation of Indonesian Chefs Go to Hone Their Craft
dek: Bali Culinary Pastry School is developing Indonesia's next generation of chefs and pastry professionals, ready to take on global kitchens.
paras: Working in a professional kitchen is no walk in the park. Behind the scenes at every top-level restaurant, highly skilled hands busy over countertops in a constant battle against time, in a high-pressure environment where everyone must do their part. The stakes are high, and not everyone has what it takes to earn their spot in a kitchen brigade.

There are thousands of restaurants in Bali, and the food and beverage scene has evolved to become one of the island’s greatest attractions in recent years, offering dining experiences of world-class quality. But this persistently improving dining scene demands a workforce of equal rank, a constant regeneration of astute culinary professionals ready to work in – and increasingly, lead – the top kitchens on the island.

Fortunately, someone had the foresight to predict this demand a decade ago, starting an industry-focused training centre in Bali where aspiring chefs and pastry professionals now go to hone their skills.

First established in 2016, Bali Culinary Pastry School (BCPS) began with just six students. In a decade the school has trained more 1,000 graduates, with students coming from 66 cities across Indonesia, as well as 12 nationalities from abroad. But this is no mere hospitality school, focused on high-level vocational skills students have gone on to train at prestigious venues across the world. Since 2023, 60 students completed six-month internships in renowned kitchens in France, Italy to Hong Kong, including Relais & Châteaux establishments and Michelin-starred restaurants.

A recent success story from 2025 saw graduate Yovita Ariandini take on a full-time position as Commis de Cuisine at the legendary Restaurant Paul Bocuse, in Lyon, France, after her internship there. She is the first Indonesian to work at this historic, Michelin-starred restaurant.

The school’s purpose-built campus is found within a large educational complex known as ‘BITDeC’ (Bali International Training and Development Centre), a sprawling facility set amid the greenery of Nyanyi, Tabanan, near Nyanyi Beach. The vision behind this family-run complex, which also hosts Politeknik Internasional Bali, was to open opportunities outside of the traditional education paths, especially for less privileged youths.
BCPS Founder, Made Ariani Siswanto, sought to fulfil that vision through high-level, industry-focused culinary training.

“BCPS was built on the belief that education is a form of stewardship — a way to preserve legacy while giving the next generation the skills, confidence, and global perspective to move forward. Inspired by my late father’s vision for BITDeC, BCPS continues to grow as a place where young people are given real opportunities to transform their lives and contribute meaningfully to the world, while remaining grounded in Balinese values,” she shares with NOW! Bali.

The facilities are impressive, with state-of-the-art culinary “Labs”, as they call them: kitchens, pastry and chocolate labs, baking learning centres all replicating professional settings. As for the curriculum, this was designed under the guidance of M.O.F. (Meilleur Ouvrier de France) Christophe Quantin as the school’s pedagogical advisor.

The schools daily teaching approach is inspired by French philosophical practices of savoir-faire and savoir-être, combining technical skills with the right professional attitude. Beyond learning recipes and techniques, students must learn how to work, think, communicate and perform in a professional environment, helping them build the skills and mindset needed once they begin work.

Perhaps most intriguing is how the school has integrated real-world experiences into the campus. At the BCPS restaurant, open to the public every lunchtime, students man the kitchen and put their lessons into practice. They develop and prepare a daily set menu, witnessing firsthand the trials and challenges of developing a restaurant experience.

This is taken to new heights at KŌRO Bali, a gastronomy dining experience at Nyanyi Beach, where students must learn directly in a live restaurant environment, alongside professional chefs and mentors. Under the leadership of KŌRO Co-founder Chef Eric Cocollos, students are assigned to specific stations and must meet the high-level demands of the kitchen. During their time there, they’re also introduce to wider restaurant operations, including service and guest interaction, allowing them to develop an understanding of hospitality beyond the kitchen as well.

title: The Ultimate Adventure in Bali: Nature, Thrills and the Great Outdoors
dek: Searching for your next adventure in Bali? Here are our recommendations, from mountain climbing to exploring national parks to jungle buggies
paras: For thrill-seekers and nature enthusiasts, this island is the ultimate playground. From volcanoes to river valleys, waterfalls to a sprawling national park, the rugged environment beckons with opportunities for exploration and adventure in Bali.

Bali sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, a hotbed of tectonic activity that has over millennia forged the magnificent landscapes of the island. Four principal volcanic mountains, gaping calderas with towering peaks and ridges, and highland lakes that feed the hundreds of rivers which have carved the dramatic ravines and poured over flood plains – these have all contributed to what can only be described as a truly awesome environment.

Add to that a fertile, tropical climate and the ecology thus thrives with thick forests that to this day blanket much of inland Bali. This is what awaits the hikers and trekkers, mountain cyclists and white water rafters. These enticing environments are an opportunity to ‘get out the south’ and to venture to distant destinations.

As mentioned, there are four principal mountains on Bali – Mt. Agung, Mt. Batur, Mt. Batukaru and Mt. Abang – but there are more than 20 significant peaks in total on the island. Each of these present their own unique terrain, and a new summit to conquer. Here are two from Bali’s eastern Karangasem Regency that tease what a mountain hike has in store.

Bali’s holiest mountain – and therefore the most important mountain on Bali. Home to Pura Besakih, the mother temple that climbs up the southern face of Agung, all Balinese Hindu must make pilgrimage to this great temple complex.
For adventure seekers, the climb to the mountain’s crater rim, battling thick mountain forest and volcanic terrain, is perhaps Bali’s most epic outdoor mission.

There are two regular routes for hikers, the first from Pura Pasar Agung Temple (1,700m above sea level) takes around 4 to 5 hours to the crater. This is normally the route taken for those doing the sunrise trek to the crater which starts at 2am. This is a direct ascent and is a steep hike up and down the mountain face. Another route, starting closer to Besakih Temple, takes around 5 to 7 hours depending on your level of fitness.

Either way, the trek up Agung is a challenging feat, first through thick mountain forests, and when the tree line ends, the volcano’s craggy crown calls for scrambling upon brush and rock. But at the top, balancing upon the boulders that line the summit edge, the most majestic view of the entire island makes every step worth it – the very contours of the coastline visible from this most epic perch.

Bali’s most eastern mountain peak, Lempuyang is best known for its Agung-facing temple where the iconic ‘Gates of Heaven’ photo is often taken. Whilst visitors line up for their photos, a more rewarding experience is found on the southeast side of Lempuyang – a forgiving trek through light, lush woodlands with gentle slopes to the top.

There is a clear path through the mountain forest, as this is an important pilgrimage for many Balinese Hindu, who walk with their offerings from the start point at Pura Jumenang towards Pura Penataran Lempuyang Puncak – the temple at the summit. Thus, shrines dot the 2.5 hour ascent, before reaching the peak, which stands at 1,174 metres above sea level.
For any mountain treks, we strongly recommend local mountain guide (and Balinese Priest), Pak Mudi: @mudigoestothemountain | mudigoestothemountain.com

Whilst many mountain trails are a journey to the peak, the trekking experience with the Muntigunung Community Development Program (MCDP) is a dramatic descent down the mountainside towards the island’s northern coastline.

title: New Faces, New Flavours: Meet the Two New Culinary Leaders at the Hyatts of Sanur
dek: Meet Hyatt Regency Bali and Andaz Bali's new culinary leaders, Ivan Gutierrez and Chef Vincenzo Gatti, elevating Sanur dining experiences.
paras: Two of Sanur’s iconic resorts, Hyatt Regency Bali and Andaz Bali, welcome new leaders set to steer future dining experiences and offerings: Ivan Gutierrez as Cluster Director of Food and Beverage, and Chef Vincenzo Gatti, now Cluster Executive Chef.

Whilst Chef Vincenzo and Ivan are newcomers on the shores of Sanur, they are both Hyatt veterans, bringing with them years of experience in global hospitality which they have already begun to implement in their respective roles across the two properties.

Ivan Gutierrez arrives from his most recent position at the Grand Hyatt Erawan Bangkok, where he served as the Director of Food and Beverage. Prior to that he held leadership roles across Asia – from Grand Hyatt Tokyo to Hyatt Regency Qingdao – working with a diverse clientele as well as portfolio of dining concepts.

As the Cluster Director of Food and Beverage, Ivan will focus on the guest experience across the two resorts’ multiple dining venues. This means delivering true hospitality, which Ivan strong believes is all about people – connecting with guests, creating meaningful experiences and memories, and ensuring that colleagues too are embodying that same spirit of hospitality.

Chef Vincenzo Gatti also arrives from a previous position in Thailand, as the Executive Chef at Andaz Pattaya Jomtien Beach. There he brought Guide Michelin recognition to two of the resort’s restaurants, La Cucina Italian Restaurant and Fish Club Seafood Restaurant. But his full Hyatt careers spans a decade, leading kitchens in prestigious properties across China and South Korea. As such, Chef Vincenzo brings with him experience of a variety of cuisines, sure to be an asset in his new role as Cluster Executive Chef at Andaz Bali and Hyatt Regency Bali.

No strangers to Hyatt, hospitality, nor a popular tourism destinations like Bali, both Ivan and Chef Vincenzo have settled quickly into the rhythm of Sanur. In their respective positions, the two culinary heads will drive the food and beverage offerings across seven distinct restaurants, from Hyatt Regency’s iconic beachfront Pizzaria to the row of restaurants within Andaz Bali’s Village Square. These are already well-loved restaurants, lauded as venues that embody that warm spirit of Sanur and celebrating local flavours – no doubt returning and first-time guests will be looking forward to seeing what Ivan and Chef Vincenzo have in store!

title: Riserva Steakhouse Opens in Ubud With an Evening in Seven Chapters
dek: Designed around An Evening in Seven Chapters, RISERVA creates an Ubud fine dining steakhouse experience that begins before the first course.
paras: Designed around An Evening in Seven Chapters, RISERVA opens as the newest addition to The Wonderspace portfolio, combining premium cuts, fine wines, and a sequence of Balinese-inspired rituals to create a fine-dining steakhouse experience in Ubud that begins long before the first course reaches the table.

The experience begins with the setting itself, as RISERVA welcomes guests when the sun sets over the valley. A series of arrival rituals unfold, beginning with a Gong Ritual, followed by a Foot Wash Ritual and Seven Tirta and Final Purification. Then, guests continue with a personalised Wariga experience, before being presented with Welcome Canapés, or Lungsuran, and a welcome drink.

A ceremonial Champagne Sabrage marks the transition into the dining experience. Progression is intentionally unhurried, allowing each stage of the evening to have its own moment, reflecting RISERVA’s belief that fine dining is about how the experience unfolds as much as it is about what is served.

At the heart of the menu is Chef Putu Armen, whose approach centres on premium ingredients and wagyu cuts, each cut bringing a different texture and level of richness to the table. This allows diners to explore the natural character of premium beef rather than just choosing between the usual steakhouse staples.

Further elevating the steak course are two rituals: Seven Knives and Seven Salts. Seven Knives presents a collection inspired by Bali’s pande heritage of master metal artisans, so guests get to choose their preferred knife for the meal; while Seven Salts introduces a selection of artisanal salts sourced from Bali and around the world, including Tejakula salt from North Bali.

Curated by Sommelier I Putu Erawan Ari Widhiantika, Bali Best Sommelier 2025, the wine programme spans established regions across Europe, the Americas, Oceania and South Africa. At the table, Chef Putu guides diners through considered pairings, while the restaurant’s Coravin programme allows guests to explore a wider selection by the glass without committing to a full bottle.

The evening does not end with the final savoury course. Guests are invited to continue the experience at Aura Lounge, where petit desserts and crafted cocktails provide a relaxed finale against the surrounding valley landscape. As part of the intent to slow down instead of rushing through dinner, the transition from dining room to lounge gives guests space to linger and let the evening unfold at its own pace.

Although RISERVA is located within Equipoise Resort, the restaurant operates as an independent dining destination and welcomes resort guests and visitors alike from across Bali. With only 16 guests accommodated per evening and one seating each night, reservations are essential.

For those seeking a different take on Ubud fine dining, RISERVA presents a premium steakhouse where an intimate evening of Balinese rituals, quality ingredients, good wine and warm hospitality come together in seven chapters.
For more information or reservations, please contact +62 813 1703 631 or email equipoiseresort@inivie.com

title: Bejana by Petty Elliott: A New Chapter in Indonesian Culinary Heritage
dek: Bejana by Petty Elliott reflects a shared commitment to preserve the rich stories and traditions that make Indonesian cuisine so diverse.
paras: At The Ritz-Carlton, Bali, Indonesian cuisine takes centre stage at Bejana, where the flavours, traditions, and stories of the archipelago come together in an elegant dining setting. The resort’s signature Indonesian restaurant now welcomes a new chapter with Bejana by Petty Elliott, a collaboration that celebrates the depth and diversity of Indonesia’s culinary heritage.

Named after the traditional vessel used to prepare and serve food, Bejana has long invited diners to discover Indonesia through its regional cuisine. The collaboration with renowned chef, author and culinary advocate Petty Elliott builds on this vision, bringing almost three decades of experience championing Indonesian food to the table.

Developed alongside The Ritz-Carlton, Bali's culinary team, the new menu takes a considered approach to traditional dishes, allowing their authentic flavours and regional identities to shine. Local sourcing remains central, with fresh seafood arriving daily from Kedonganan fishermen, beef sourced from local producers, and vegetables, herbs and spices selected from farmers across Bali.

Among the highlights is Red Snapper with Bumbu Woku, featuring freshly caught snapper wrapped in banana leaves and served with locally grown pakis, or fiddlehead fern. Inspired by North Sulawesi, the aromatic woku spice blend shares several herbs and spices with Bali’s bumbu genep, creating a connection between two distinct culinary traditions.

The menu also celebrates Indonesia’s plant-based heritage with Tempe Satay, where locally produced tempeh is prepared using the traditional bacem method before being grilled over charcoal for a sweet, savoury and smoky finish.

The collaboration will be officially celebrated with a special menu unveiling on 24 August 2026, beginning with sunset aperitifs, Indonesian-inspired canapés, traditional rindik music, and Balinese dance performances. Guests will then be invited into Bejana's Culinary Cave for an immersive dinner, with selected dishes presented from live culinary stations and opportunities to connect with the chefs.

“Indonesian cuisine is incredibly layered,” explains Petty Elliott. “Every island, every community, and every family has its own way of telling a story through food. At Bejana, we wanted to honour those traditions with sincerity – allowing the ingredients, the techniques, and the regional identities to speak for themselves.”

Bejana by Petty Elliott reflects a shared commitment that goes beyond mere collaboration to preserve the stories and traditions that make Indonesian cuisine so diverse. Through respect for cooking, sourcing, and regional heritage, the restaurant offers diners the opportunity to experience the archipelago's genuine flavours, one dish at a time.
For more information or reservations, please contact +62 368 498 988 or visit bejanaindonesianrestaurant.com

title: Sanur's New Lamuri Explores the Culinary Ties of South India and Sumatra
dek: Sanur welcomes an intriguing new restaurant, Lamuri, that invites diners to explore the culinary relationship between South India and North Sumatra.
paras: Sanur welcomes an intriguing new restaurant, Lamuri, that invites diners to explore the culinary relationship between South India and Sumatra.

Lamuri is inspired by an historic kingdom that was located on the northern tip of Sumatra – now modern-day Aceh – between the 9th and 16th centuries. Also known as Lambri, the ancient kingdom was a major trading port, opening to the Andaman Sea, Bay of Bengal and Indian Ocean, connecting the region to global maritime traders – and as a consequence, influence from Sri Lanka, India and beyond.

Chef-founder Aman Lakhiani revisits this history through a culinary lens, developing a menu that showcases South Indian, Sri Lankan and Sumatran flavours, exploring a spectrum of shared ingredients to distinct dishes of these regions. Utilising local Indonesian ingredients, paired with Indian spices, the flavours are rich, aromatic and complex.

Highlights include Kare Kambing, a slow-cooked mutton curry steeped in Sumatran and South Indian spices; Kothu Roti, a favourite Sri Lankan street food of chopped flatbread tossed with the spiced curry gravy; Crab Masala, where coconut richness and South Indian masala seeps into sweet crab meat; and Ayam Tangkap Aceh, a fragrant fried chicken specialty representing the Sumatran side of Lamuri.

Meals are best enjoyed family-style, where dishes are shared and passed around the table, set over banana leaves to capture a traditional dining style. Rattan seats, terracotta-coloured walls, and the joglo-style ceiling speak to the restaurant’s regional theme, with the wood-panelled open, kitchen and stylish bar area giving the interiors a contemporary edge.

title: Eyerizz Eyewear: One-Stop Solution for Prescription Glasses in Bali

paras: Whether you've broken your favourite frames on holiday, need a new pair of sunglasses, or want to update your eyewear while in Bali, finding a reliable optical store can make all the difference. For visitors unsure where to begin, the optical team can help narrow down the choices based on face shape, personal style, lifestyle and prescription. Having cultivated a strong reputation and customer base, Eyerizz offers a practical combo of professional optical services, an extensive selection, and traveller-friendly convenience for anyone needing prescription glasses in Bali.
